name: Future/Promise
intent: Start slow work now and get a placeholder for its result, so other work can go on and the value is used when it arrives.
scenario: A product page needs a price from one service and a stock level from another. Each lookup is slow, and the stock service sometimes fails.
problem: The code asks for the price and waits, then asks for the stock and waits, so the page takes the sum of both lookups. One failure in the second lookup also throws away the price that had already arrived.
solution: Starting a lookup returns a future at once: an object that stands for a value that is not there yet. The caller starts both lookups, then waits for the futures together. The work that fills in the value holds the promise, the write side: when it finishes, it sets the result or the error, and every waiter is released. Combine several futures to wait for all of them, for the first, or to keep whatever succeeded.
pain: Each lookup blocks until it finishes before the next one starts
The page waits for the sum of the lookup times
A failure in a later lookup discards earlier results
Callbacks nested inside callbacks make the flow hard to read
benefits: Independent work runs at the same time
The wait is about the slowest lookup, not the sum
Each result or error is a value that can be inspected on its own
Code reads in order with await, with no nested callbacks
whenToUse: Work is slow because it waits for something: a network, a disk or another service
Several pieces of work are independent and can be started together
You want to combine results, or to react to each one as it finishes
whenNotToUse: Work that is fast and local: the machinery costs more than the wait
Steps where each needs the previous result: there is nothing to run at the same time
Work that is heavy on the CPU: futures alone do not use more cores
pitfalls: An error nobody awaits can disappear, or crash the process as an unhandled rejection
Starting thousands of futures at once can overload the service they call: limit the concurrency
Waiting for all with fail-on-first throws away the results that did succeed
A future that never completes makes its waiter hang for ever, so put timeouts on waits

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: Starts the work, keeps the futures and later waits for them.

roles.label: Future
roles.description: The read side: a handle for a value that is not there yet. It can be waited on or given a continuation.

roles.label: Promise
roles.description: The write side: a handle that the producing work uses to set the value or the error exactly once.

roles.label: Continuation
roles.description: Code that runs when the future completes: combine the results, show them or handle the error.

quiz.question: A page awaits a price lookup (250 ms) and then a stock lookup (250 ms) that does not need the price. The page takes 500 ms. What is the best change?
options: Cache both values for an hour so that most visitors skip the lookups
Start both lookups first, keep their futures, then await both together
Make each lookup twice as fast with a bigger server for the price service
Use callbacks instead of await so that the page does not block on the lookups
quiz.explanation: The lookups are independent, so the second does not need to wait for the first. Starting both and awaiting them together takes about 250 ms. Caching shows stale values, a bigger server helps only one lookup, and callbacks without starting both early still run them in turn.

quiz.question: A page loads three panels with Promise.all. The third service fails, and the user sees an error page, although the first two panels loaded fine. What is the best fix?
options: Retry the whole Promise.all until all three succeed, then show the page
Remove the third panel from the page, so that the failure can no longer happen
Increase the timeout of the third lookup so that it is less likely to fail
Settle each future on its own, show the panels that worked, and handle the failed one
quiz.explanation: Promise.all fails as soon as one future fails, and the other results are dropped. Waiting for each future to settle (allSettled, or catching per future) keeps what worked. Retrying everything repeats the failure, removing the panel loses the feature, and a longer timeout does not remove errors.

quiz.question: A job starts one future for each of 50,000 records at once, and the database it calls begins to refuse connections. What is the best fix?
options: Limit how many futures run at a time, for example with a pool or a semaphore of 20
Start the futures one after another and await each, so that only one runs
Increase the database's connection limit until it accepts 50,000 requests at once
Ignore the errors, since the futures that were refused will be retried by the system
quiz.explanation: Futures make it easy to start too much at once. A concurrency limit keeps the parallelism and protects the database. Awaiting one by one gives up the speed-up, a huge connection limit only moves the problem, and refused futures are not retried by themselves.
